title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
blurb: Morgan Housel argues that managing money is less like physics and more like psychology. It is a soft skill, where behavior matters more than intelligence or technical knowledge. Through a series of short stories, he shows that people make money choices based on their own life experiences, so no one is truly crazy. He explains how luck and risk shape every outcome, why compounding rewards patience over brilliance, and why staying wealthy needs different habits than getting wealthy. Housel shows that real wealth is the money you don't spend and can't see. He also argues that knowing when you have enough protects you from ruin. Above all, he says money's greatest value is the freedom to control your own time. The book offers a humble, practical way to think about saving, investing, and living well.

lessons.t: No One Is Crazy About Money
lessons.b: Everyone's money decisions make sense to them because they are shaped by the particular slice of history and experience each person has lived through.
Outcomes are never purely the result of our decisions, so we should be humble about success and forgiving about failure, both our own and others'.
Compounding rewards staying invested for a very long time far more than finding the highest returns, which is why patience beats brilliance.
Getting wealthy takes optimism and risk, but staying wealthy takes caution, frugality, and enough room for error to survive the bad times.

lessons.t: Wealth Is What You Don't See
lessons.b: True wealth is the money left unspent, so flashy possessions often signal less wealth, not more, and rarely earn the admiration people hope for.
